newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ markets seize soft GDP as herald of more easing.
newsitem.headline: NZ markets seize soft GDP as herald of more easing.

text.p: New Zealand financial markets leapt into action on Monday after Gross Domestic Product (GDP) data confirmed the appropriateness of looser monetary conditions as sanctioned by the central bank last week.

The stock market's top-40 index surged 2.4 percent to an all-time high of 2,501 points, the Kiwi dollar shed a quarter of a cent against the U.S. dollar to US$0.6778, and interest rates resumed their downward journey, though at a meandering pace.
The flurry was triggered by the first quarterly contraction of the New Zealand economy since September 1992.

Analysts said a 0.5 percent fall in March quarter GDP showed how flat economic activity has been this year, which augured well for further rallies on prospects for an even easier monetary environment under the Reserve Bank of New Zealand.
"If we continue to see a run of weaker activity and inflation data, then the market might look to price in even greater amounts of easing," said ANZ bank chief economist Paul Stewart.

Market expectations had been for a 0.1 percent fall in March quarter GDP. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's (RBNZ) forecast was significantly higher, at plus 0.3 percent, but analysts said the data showed just how accurate the RBNZ's easing call was in its statement on Friday.

The RBNZ eased monetary policy by 100 basis points for the September quarter, signalled the likelihood of a further 40-point easing in the December quarter, and said it could live with conditions 50 points either side of its desired level.
The statement surprised commentators, who had anticipated an easing of a smaller magnitude.
But the GDP result unleashed a flood of new predictions for even easier conditions, and a wave of optimism that growth prospects would improve.
"To the extent that today's result encourages the market or the RBNZ to ease further, growth prospects could improve," said Bankers Trust chief economist David Plank.
The March quarter GDP result may have been affected by the timing of the Easter Holiday and the absence of a leap year, which combined to reduce trading days in the quarter by five percent, he said.
But the RBNZ would focus on combined growth over the March and June 1997 quarters, which looked likely to be lower than the bank's 0.6 percent forecast.
"This will reinforce the RBNZ's easing bias," Plank added.
Bankers Trust believes the generally positive inflation outlook will see the Kiwi dollar weaken on its Trade-Weighted Index to 65.0 by year end.
The TWI shed 20 points after the GDP release to 66.70.

Stock brokers said the equities market was relishing its new, friendlier platform of a lower currency and lower interest rates, and was looking for more of the same to boost exporters and domestic companies trying to invest for growth.
However, economists stressed the need for the GDP data to be placed within a wider context.
Indicators of current conditions, such as business confidence surveys, would be keenly observed and the June quarter Consumer Price Index due on July 15 was seen as a key.

While conditions conducive to growth looked to be shaping, Treasury's growth forecasts for next year remain optimistic in many observers' eyes, and concerns about the fiscal prudence of the government's planned NZ$5 billion spending package remain.
